blocks.text: When the body needs to conserve water the kidneys excrete hypertonic urine, and when there is much water they excrete hypotonic urine. Two hormones coordinate this.

ADH is the body's main tool for saving water. It is made by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary gland. When the body is dehydrated or has eaten salty food, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the higher salt concentration of the blood. The hypothalamus then creates a sensation of thirst and signals the posterior pituitary to release ADH. ADH makes the walls of the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water moves from the filtrate into the salty fluid and then into the blood: concentrated urine is made and water is conserved.

When the salt concentration of the blood falls, the hypothalamus stops ADH secretion. The collecting duct walls become less permeable, less water is reabsorbed and dilute urine is excreted; blood volume and blood pressure fall.

blocks.title: Diabetes insipidus
blocks.text: A person who cannot make enough ADH because of damage to the pituitary constantly passes a large volume of dilute urine. This disorder is diabetes insipidus; the person is in danger of severe dehydration and very low blood pressure.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: ADH raises blood volume and so blood pressure. It also makes blood vessels constrict (narrow), which raises blood pressure further.

Aldosterone regulates the sodium and potassium levels of urine. It is produced by the adrenal cortex, the outer layer of the adrenal gland on top of the kidney. It is secreted when blood pressure drops or blood sodium is too low. It acts on the walls of the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct and increases the reabsorption of sodium ions from the filtrate into the blood; because the blood then holds more sodium, water also moves from the filtrate into the blood.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Aldosterone also promotes the excretion of potassium ions in urine. This helps prevent hyperkalaemia, a dangerously high blood potassium level that can cause cardiac arrhythmias.
